specPoints.text: describe how glasshouses and polythene tunnels can be used to increase the yield of certain crops

primer.text: A glasshouse is a climate machine, and a polythene tunnel is its budget cousin. This note shows how enclosing a crop lets a farmer steer the factors that limit photosynthesis, lists the controls inside a glasshouse, explains the cost-versus-income judgement, and covers what tunnels shield crops from.

lessons.title: Glasshouses: Engineering the Weather
lessons.opening: Inside a glasshouse the farmer replaces the weather with a set of dials. Artificial heating, artificial lighting, enriched carbon dioxide and regular watering each push photosynthesis along, and the grower keeps the receipts balanced against the extra income the bigger crop brings.
keyPoints: Artificial heating warms the air so the enzymes driving photosynthesis work faster, a measure used mainly in temperate countries.
Artificial lighting extends the hours a crop can photosynthesise each day.
Raising the carbon dioxide content of the greenhouse air speeds the reaction further.
Regular watering keeps water supply off the list of constraints.
Every control costs money, so the farmer balances spending on heat, light and carbon dioxide against the extra income from higher yield.
In hot tropical regions glasshouses may need vents opened to shed heat before enzymes denature.

low.restatement: Warm it, light it, feed it carbon dioxide, water it — then check the extra crop pays the heating bill.
low.analogy: Turning a field into a car with the climate control stuck on perfect.
low.examPointer: Always finish cost questions with the balance phrase: extra cost weighed against increased income.

medium.restatement: A glasshouse lets the grower raise temperature, extend light, enrich carbon dioxide and water regularly, so photosynthesis runs closer to its potential; the decision rule is comparing the added cost of each control with the added income from the yield, and tropical growers vent their structures to avoid enzyme damage.
medium.analogy: A chef adjusting the oven, the lamps and the seasoning all at once, charging enough for the dish to pay for the kitchen.
medium.examPointer: Name denaturation when explaining why tropical glasshouses are ventilated — the enzymes controlling photosynthesis fail when overheated.

check.stem: Why does artificial heating raise photosynthesis inside a glasshouse?

options.text: The enzymes controlling the reaction work faster when warmer, within limits
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Heat converts light into sugar directly
options.explanation: Light capture and heat are separate inputs.

options.text: Warm air holds more carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide enrichment is a separate control.

options.text: Roots absorb warmer water faster
options.explanation: Root uptake is not the mechanism cited.

check.stem: What advantage does artificial lighting give a protected crop?

options.text: Photosynthesis can continue for more hours each day
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The crop needs less watering
options.explanation: Watering is controlled separately.

options.text: The glass becomes stronger
options.explanation: Lighting has no structural effect.

options.text: Pests are repelled by brightness
options.explanation: Pest exclusion is not the role of lamps.

check.stem: Why must a glasshouse farmer compare costs before switching controls on?

options.text: Heating, lighting and carbon dioxide enrichment all cost money that the extra yield must repay
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Regulators forbid running controls in summer
options.explanation: No such rule governs glasshouse practice.

options.text: Controls damage the crop when combined
options.explanation: The controls complement one another.

options.text: Costs never change with yield
options.explanation: The whole judgement is cost against income.

check.stem: Why might a tropical glasshouse be ventilated rather than heated?

options.text: Venting sheds excess heat so photosynthetic enzymes avoid denaturation
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Ventilation brings in extra carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Venting releases air; enrichment is handled separately.

options.text: Tropical sun is too weak for crops
options.explanation: Tropical light is intense, not weak.

options.text: Vents keep the glass clean
options.explanation: Cleaning is not the purpose of ventilation.

check.stem: In which countries is artificial glasshouse heating most used?

options.text: Temperate countries such as the United Kingdom
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Only tropical countries
options.explanation: Tropical regions more often need cooling.

options.text: Desert countries with year-round sun
options.explanation: Desert light and heat rarely call for heating.

options.text: Countries at the equator
options.explanation: Equatorial climates are already warm.

check.stem: List the four conditions a glasshouse grower can control to lift yield.
check.modelAnswer: Temperature through heating, light through lamps, carbon dioxide enrichment of the air, and regular watering.

check.stem: State the financial rule a glasshouse farmer applies to each control.
check.modelAnswer: The extra cost of providing each condition is balanced against the increased income from the bigger crop.

check.stem: Explain why an enclosed environment raises yields compared with open fields.
check.modelAnswer: Enclosure lets the farmer hold each limiting factor nearer its optimum, so photosynthesis runs faster for longer and the crop builds more biomass than any open field would allow.

check.stem: A grower's heating bill doubles but tomato prices triple. Advise on the heating control and justify the advice.
check.modelAnswer: Run the heating, because the increased income from selling warm-season tomatoes at high prices outweighs the extra cost of the fuel.

lessons.title: Polythene Tunnels and Protected Crops
sourceHeadings: Limiting factors and the growth of crop plants
lessons.opening: A polythene tunnel is the field crop's raincoat and blanket at once. The plastic skin shelters plants from wind, rain and temperature extremes, traps a little extra warmth, and bars the entry of many pests and diseases that would otherwise chew through the yield.
keyPoints: Knowledge of limiting factors tells the farmer which conditions most restrict photosynthesis outdoors.
Tunnels protect outdoor crops from excessive wind, rain and extreme temperatures.
The plastic covering raises the temperature inside the tunnel slightly.
Tunnels also block many pests and diseases from reaching the plants.

low.restatement: A big plastic sleeve over the crop: warm inside, storms outside, bugs mostly locked out.
low.analogy: A raincoat worn by an entire field instead of one person.
low.examPointer: Give both protection jobs — weather and pests — when asked why tunnels raise yields.

medium.restatement: Because farmers know which factors limit photosynthesis, they use polythene tunnels to moderate them: the plastic holds warmth, shields plants from wind, rain and temperature extremes, and excludes many pests and disease carriers from the crop.
medium.analogy: A greenhouse shrunk and stretched over a field row, wearing thin so the sun still reaches the leaves.
medium.examPointer: Contrast tunnels with glasshouses briefly — tunnels protect and warm but offer fewer dials than a full glasshouse.

check.stem: Which weather threats does a polythene tunnel shield a crop from?

options.text: Excessive wind, heavy rain and extreme temperatures
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Snowfall alone
options.explanation: Snow is one case, but the protection is broader.

options.text: Only strong sunshine
options.explanation: Shade cloth, not polythene, manages sunshine.

options.text: Frost exclusively
options.explanation: Frost protection is one benefit among several.

check.stem: What happens to the air temperature inside a polythene tunnel?

options.text: It rises slightly above the outside temperature
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It falls below outdoor levels
options.explanation: The covering traps warmth, it does not cool.

options.text: It matches the open field exactly
options.explanation: The whole point is a modest lift.

options.text: It climbs to glasshouse extremes
options.explanation: Tunnels warm less than managed glasshouses.

check.stem: How does a tunnel help with pests?

options.text: It prevents many pests from entering and reaching the plants
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: It poisons insects on contact
options.explanation: The plastic is a barrier, not a poison.

options.text: It attracts pests away from the crop
options.explanation: No attraction mechanism operates.

options.text: It drowns eggs during rain
options.explanation: Rain is excluded rather than weaponised.

check.stem: Which knowledge lets a farmer decide what to improve first for an outdoor crop?

options.text: Understanding which limiting factors most restrict photosynthesis
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Guessing from the colour of the polythene
options.explanation: Colour choice is cosmetic.

options.text: Counting the number of plants per row
options.explanation: Plant spacing is a separate management question.

options.text: Reading last year's market prices
options.explanation: Prices guide selling, not plant physiology.

check.stem: A salad grower wants earlier spring crops in a windy valley. Which structure fits best?

options.text: A polythene tunnel, which warms and shelters the crop
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: An open field with extra watering
options.explanation: Open ground leaves the crop exposed.

options.text: A shaded lorry cover
options.explanation: Crops need light, not vehicle shade.

options.text: Deeper seed drilling
options.explanation: Drilling depth does not block wind.

check.stem: State two protective jobs a polythene tunnel does for a crop.
check.modelAnswer: It shields plants from harsh weather such as wind and rain, and it keeps many pests and diseases out.

check.stem: Name the structure that gives a farmer more control than a tunnel.
check.modelAnswer: A glasshouse offers the farmer greater control over conditions than a polythene tunnel.

check.stem: Explain why the slight warmth inside a tunnel still benefits the crop.
check.modelAnswer: Even a small temperature rise lets photosynthetic enzymes work faster, so the crop grows quicker than plants left in the open cold.

check.stem: Hail is forecast for a lettuce field under no protection and one under a tunnel. Predict the outcome difference.
check.modelAnswer: The tunnel crop escapes the hailstones that would shred the exposed lettuces, so the protected yield survives while the open field suffers losses.

glossary.definition: An enclosed, transparent structure in which crop climate can be controlled.
A large plastic tunnel laid over field crops to shelter and warm them.
The factor in shortest supply that caps the rate of photosynthesis.
Deliberate airing of a structure to release excess heat.
